strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: prior hierarchical alignment methods use a single visual feature against hierarchical text features, creating an asymmetric alignment; this paper proposes a principled symmetric solution by constructing hierarchical visual features via a text-guided cross-attention over intermediate ViT layers.

Provides a non-trivial theoretical contribution: an approximate KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions on hyperbolic manifolds with different curvatures, used to define a manifold distance and derive an intermediate manifold with proven existence/uniqueness (Theorem 1, Propositions 1-2), plus a practical optimization scheme using golden section search and the implicit function theorem for curvature gradients.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four datasets (CIFAR100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), multiple settings (1-shot, 16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), and two backbone prompt-tuning methods (MaPLe, PromptSRC), with consistent and often large improvements over strong baselines including ProTeCt, MERU, and HyCoCLIP.

Thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of the semantic-aware visual feature extraction, hyperbolic alignment, and heterogeneous manifold search components, supporting the claimed design choices.

Good supplementary analysis via t-SNE visualization of learned representations and GradCAM attention maps showing hierarchy-consistent, biologically meaningful attention patterns across taxonomic levels.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing (including a nontrivial tree-construction procedure for Rare Species), and stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: The core KL-divergence approximation relies on a Taylor expansion around a numerically found point y1≈3.016 chosen to zero out a derivative at c3=c1; this is a somewhat ad hoc approximation whose global tightness/validity away from this specific regime is not rigorously justified, and Propositions 1-2 require large-r sufficient conditions (rmin thresholds) that are not obviously satisfied during actual training, creating a gap between the theoretical guarantees and practical optimization.
There appears to be a typo/bug in Eq.(18): the update rule for c2 uses dJ/dc1 instead of dJ/dc2, raising concerns about implementation correctness or at least careless proofreading of key equations.

Comparisons with pretraining-based hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) yield very large improvement margins (up to 50%), which may partly reflect that these are zero-shot/pretrained models not fine-tuned for the TOS task, making the comparison potentially less apples-to-apples than the few-shot/prompt-tuning baselines.

The method's applicability is restricted to datasets with well-defined hierarchical/taxonomic label structures, limiting generality; three of the four datasets rely on externally imposed taxonomies (e.g., WordNet) rather than natural hierarchies, which could affect the validity of the hierarchical alignment claims.

The core technical building blocks (wrapped normal distributions, hyperbolic entailment cones, curvature learning via implicit differentiation) are adapted from prior work (Nagano et al. 2019, Desai et al. 2023, Pal et al. 2025, Lorraine et al. 2020), making the primary novel contribution the heterogeneous-curvature intermediate manifold alignment, which is a comparatively narrow, incremental technical advance.

No variance/error bars are reported in the main tables despite the paper stating results are averaged over three runs, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported gains, especially smaller ones.

Evaluation is limited to prompt-tuning adaptations of CLIP with ViT-B/16; there is no validation on larger backbones or full fine-tuning/pretraining settings, which limits confidence in generalization to broader VLM regimes.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated asymmetry problem (single visual feature vs. hierarchical textual features) and proposes a coherent pipeline combining semantic-aware hierarchical visual feature extraction with heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four datasets (Cifar100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species) and four settings (1-shot, 16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), with three metrics (LA, HCA, MTA), consistently shows improvements over ProTeCt, MaPLe, PromptSRC, and hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP).

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of the semantic-aware feature extraction, the hyperbolic constraints, and the heterogeneous manifold search (Ours-Euc, Ours-HypV1, Ours-HypV2, full model).

Attempts a theoretical justification (existence/uniqueness of an optimal intermediate curvature) rather than relying purely on heuristics, and provides an implicit-function-theorem-based gradient computation for the non-differentiable golden-section search.
Qualitative visualizations (t-SNE, GradCAM attention maps) provide some intuitive support that the hierarchical visual features attend to semantically meaningful, taxonomy-consistent regions.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result (Theorem 1) is derived via a first-order Taylor expansion of the hyperbolic distance around an essentially arbitrary/instance-dependent expansion point y1 (with a specific numerically-found value y1*≈3.016), yet the paper calls the resulting quantity D_L an exact 'affine transformation of the KL divergence.' This is an approximation, not an identity, and the subsequent 'existence and uniqueness' proofs (Propositions 1 and 2) inherit this approximation without acknowledging or quantifying the error, undermining the rigor of the central theoretical claim.

The quantity r in Theorem 1/Eq.(9) is stated to 'depend on u1 and u2' (i.e., on the actual data), yet it is treated as a fixed constant throughout the optimization objective Jc(c3) and in the proofs of Propositions 1–2, and the uniqueness proof in Appendix A.3 requires r to exceed specific large thresholds (rmin, r*min) that are not shown to hold for the actual learned/optimized r during training — so the practical validity of the 'proven' uniqueness is unclear.

The magnitude of reported improvements over hyperbolic baselines (up to 41–51% on HCA/MTA over HyCoCLIP) is very large and raises questions about whether the comparison is fair (e.g., different pretraining data/objectives, no fine-tuning of MERU/HyCoCLIP on the same downstream task), which is not adequately discussed.

The evaluation is restricted to the somewhat niche Taxonomic Open-Set classification benchmark built on top of two specific prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC); no evaluation on more standard/broader VLM benchmarks (e.g., retrieval, zero-shot ImageNet variants, general downstream tasks) is provided, limiting evidence of general significance for modality alignment in VLMs.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported despite averaging over 3 runs, and the very large gains in some settings (e.g., 16-shot Rare Species LA/HCA jumping from 48/24 to 70/54) are not accompanied by statistical significance testing.

Clarity issues: notation is dense and occasionally inconsistent (e.g., text says 'depends on u1 and u2' but formulas use u1 and u3), a typo in the section title ('REALTED WORKS'), and the paper heavily relies on appendix proofs that are difficult to fully verify, reducing overall readability and reproducibility confidence.

The method introduces considerable additional complexity (multiple learnable curvatures, golden-section search each iteration, implicit-function-theorem gradients, cross-attention over intermediate layers) without a clear computational cost/efficiency analysis compared to baselines, which is important given the practical overhead this entails.

strengths: Identifies a clear and well-motivated gap in existing hierarchical VLM alignment methods: prior work aligns hierarchical textual features with a single visual feature, creating asymmetric alignment; the paper addresses this directly with a symmetric tree-to-tree design.

Nontrivial theoretical contribution: derives an approximate KL-divergence-based distance between wrapped normal distributions on heterogeneous-curvature hyperbolic manifolds, and proves existence/uniqueness of an optimal intermediate curvature (Propositions 1 and 2), with an implicit-function-theorem-based gradient for the non-differentiable golden-section search step.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across four datasets (Cifar100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), multiple settings (1-shot, 16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), and three metrics (LA, HCA, MTA), with consistent improvements over strong baselines (MaPLe, PromptSRC, ProTeCt) and hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP).
Ablation study isolates the contribution of each component (semantic-aware visual features, hyperbolic constraints, heterogeneous manifold search), supporting the claimed design choices.

Good supplementary qualitative analysis (t-SNE and GradCAM visualizations) that plausibly supports the claim that the extracted visual features carry coarse-to-fine semantics aligned with taxonomy levels.
Detailed reproducibility appendix, including full proofs, training algorithms, and dataset preprocessing procedures.
weaknesses: The Taylor-expansion approximation used to derive a closed-form KL divergence on hyperbolic manifolds (Theorem 1) is not empirically validated; there is no experiment quantifying the approximation error against the true (intractable) KL divergence or against alternative distance surrogates.

The theoretical guarantees in Propositions 1 and 2 rely on asymptotic conditions on the parameter r (e.g., r > some large threshold derived from c1, c2, cmin) that are not checked or reported for the actual r values arising during training, leaving a gap between the stated theory and its applicability in practice.

The scalar r in Theorem 1 is described as depending on the data (via u1, u2), yet in the curvature-optimization derivation it is treated as a fixed constant; this simplification is not clearly justified and could undermine the tightness of the optimality claims.

Comparison to hyperbolic multimodal baselines is limited to only two methods (MERU, HyCoCLIP), and the reported performance gaps are extremely large (e.g., >40-50% HCA/MTA improvements), which raises questions about whether these baselines were adapted/tuned fairly for the TOS task versus being used essentially out-of-the-box.
No variance/standard deviation is reported despite averaging over three runs, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains, especially in the few-shot regime.

The evaluation is confined to a single benchmark paradigm (taxonomic open-set classification introduced by one prior paper), without demonstrating that the proposed alignment method benefits more standard/general VLM tasks such as zero-shot classification or retrieval, limiting evidence of broader significance.
Key architectural hyperparameters (choice of intermediate layers 4 and 7, number of hierarchy levels H) are fixed without an ablation showing sensitivity to these choices.

No discussion or measurement of computational overhead (e.g., training time, memory) introduced by the golden-section curvature search and implicit differentiation relative to baseline prompt-learning methods.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., a section header typo 'REALTED WORKS', table entries labeled 'villina' instead of 'vanilla') suggest the manuscript could benefit from more careful proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: asymmetric alignment between hierarchical textual features and a single visual feature in existing prompt-learning VLM methods, and proposes a symmetric tree-based alignment.

Introduces a principled way to handle heterogeneous curvatures across modalities via an intermediate hyperbolic manifold, along with theoretical results (Theorem 1, Propositions 1-2) establishing existence and uniqueness of the optimal curvature.

Extensive experiments spanning four datasets (Cifar100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), multiple task settings (1-shot, 16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), and two backbone prompt-tuning methods (MaPLe, PromptSRC), consistently showing improvements over strong baselines (ProTeCt).

Very thorough ablation studies (variant comparisons Ours-Euc/HypV1/HypV2, distance metric choices, cross-attention removal, hyperparameter sensitivity, backbone size, curvature initialization) and additional analyses (efficiency, learned curvatures per dataset, attention/t-SNE visualizations) that support the claimed contributions.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility material (proofs, algorithms, hyperparameters) and a dedicated efficiency analysis showing modest computational overhead.
weaknesses: The core theoretical distance measure (Theorem 1) is derived via a Taylor approximation with an empirically measured mean relative error of 5.3% and worst-case error up to 32.4%, which weakens the rigor of the 'existence and uniqueness' claims that are central to the paper's theoretical contribution; the approximation point y* and constant r are somewhat ad hoc.
The proposed manifold 'distance' is explicitly not a formal metric (asymmetric, violates triangle inequality), which is a nontrivial limitation for a quantity used to justify optimality claims.

Ablations (Table 3, Table 6) show that the incremental gains from the full heterogeneous manifold alignment (HypV1 -> HypV2 -> Ours) over the simpler Ours-Euc variant are often small (sometimes <1 point, occasionally negative on LA), suggesting the added geometric machinery (separate learnable curvatures, intermediate manifold search, implicit differentiation) contributes less than the semantic-aware visual feature extraction module, which somewhat undercuts the paper's central selling point.

Comparisons to general-purpose hyperbolic VLM methods (MERU, HyCoCLIP) in Appendix C.1 are against models not specifically designed/trained for taxonomic classification, making the large reported gains less informative about the specific contribution of heterogeneous curvature alignment versus simply using a task-specific hierarchical objective.

The overall method is quite complex (cross-attention hierarchical feature extraction, dual-curvature embeddings, entailment cone losses, golden-section search for intermediate curvature, implicit function theorem gradients), which raises practical reproducibility and tuning-burden concerns despite the provided algorithmic descriptions.

The datasets used for TOS classification largely rely on synthetically constructed taxonomies (e.g., via WordNet) rather than natively hierarchical datasets except Rare Species, raising questions about how well results generalize to real-world hierarchical semantics beyond the specific benchmark introduced by prior work (Wu et al., 2024).

strengths: Addresses a sensible and underexplored problem: the asymmetry between single-vector image embeddings and hierarchical text embeddings in modality alignment for taxonomic classification.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four datasets, multiple settings (1-shot, 16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole) and two prompt-tuning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), with consistent improvements over the ProTeCt baseline.

Large appendix with many ablations (variant studies, distance-metric alternatives, sensitivity to layer choice/curvature initialization/alpha, backbone scaling to ViT-L/14, class-imbalance check, efficiency analysis) and qualitative visualizations (t-SNE, GradCAM) that attempt to substantiate design choices.

Attempt at theoretical grounding (existence/uniqueness of an intermediate-curvature manifold) is a nice idea in principle, and the use of implicit differentiation to backprop through a golden-section search is a reasonable engineering solution.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution (the KL-based manifold distance D_L) relies on a first-order Taylor approximation of the hyperbolic distance around a point y1 that is then chosen specifically so that the derivative vanishes at c3=c1; Proposition 1's conclusion that the minimizer is exactly c3=c1 is therefore largely a consequence of this curve-fitting choice rather than an independent validation of the metric's soundness.

The quantity r (the Euclidean norm of a tangent-space midpoint) is derived as explicitly depending on c1 and c3 (Eq. 26), yet it is subsequently treated as a fixed constant during the optimization over c3 in Eq. 9-10; this internal inconsistency undermines the rigor of the 'proof' of existence/uniqueness built on top of it.

The empirical Taylor-approximation error analysis (Appendix C.9) reports a mean relative error of 5.3% but a maximum of 32.4%, which is a substantial deviation for a formula whose main selling point is mathematical precision/soundness.

The proposed distance is explicitly acknowledged to not be a formal metric (no symmetry, no triangle inequality), yet it is used as if it reliably measures 'manifold dissimilarity'; the practical justification for why this suffices is thin beyond the ablation in Table 8 showing marginal gains over naive alternatives (e.g., squared curvature difference).

Comparisons to other hyperbolic vision-language alignment methods (MERU, HyCoCLIP) show implausibly large gaps (e.g., HCA of ~9-26% vs. ~69% for the proposed method), suggesting these baselines were not adapted/tuned fairly for the TOS task (they are pretraining-based methods not fine-tuned with prompts on the few-shot setting), making the comparison appear more favorable than it should.

The efficiency analysis in the main text states the multi-curvature overhead is 'negligible' (74s vs 74.5s), but the appendix figure (Fig. 13) shows ~30% additional training time and higher memory relative to the ProTeCt baseline overall, which is a more meaningful and non-negligible cost that is downplayed in the main text.

Evaluation is restricted entirely to a single narrow task (taxonomic open-set classification on a handful of datasets with synthetically or WordNet-derived hierarchies), which is a weak proxy for the much broader claim in the title and abstract about 'modality alignment' in VLMs generally; no evaluation on standard zero-shot/retrieval/VQA benchmarks is provided to support the broader claim.

Many core building blocks (wrapped normal distributions, hyperbolic entailment cones, curvature learning via implicit differentiation) are directly reused from prior work (Nagano et al., Desai et al., Gao et al., Lorraine et al.), and the genuinely new pieces (cross-attention-based coarse-to-fine visual tree construction, the approximate KL manifold distance) are each individually incremental, raising concerns about the overall novelty relative to the complexity of the proposed pipeline.

The method requires the number of extracted visual hierarchy levels to match the textual taxonomy depth H, tying the architecture to the specific dataset's annotated hierarchy structure, which limits generality and is only partially acknowledged in the limitations section.

The paper's heavy reliance on ~20 pages of appendix (proofs, extra tables, extra visualizations) to defend basic design decisions and theoretical claims suggests the core paper is not self-contained and that many of its claims need extensive post-hoc patching to appear convincing.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the asymmetry between hierarchical textual features and single-vector visual features in modality alignment for VLMs.

Technically creative combination of ideas: semantic-aware coarse-to-fine visual feature extraction via cross-attention over intermediate ViT layers, combined with heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment via an intermediate manifold.

Provides theoretical grounding (Theorem 1, Propositions 1-2) for the existence and uniqueness of the optimal intermediate curvature, with full proofs in the appendix, which is a nontrivial and welcome addition compared to purely empirical hyperbolic alignment papers.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 datasets, multiple settings (1-shot, 16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), two prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), and comparisons against strong/recent hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP), showing consistent and often substantial improvements (e.g., up to 28.83% HCA gain in 16-shot).

Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions of the semantic-aware extraction module vs. the hyperbolic alignment/intermediate manifold search, plus sensitivity analyses on layer choice, curvature initialization, loss weight, and the Taylor approximation constant r.

Good supplementary analyses: efficiency/overhead measurement (negligible cost for multi-curvature learning), attention-map and t-SNE visualizations that are biologically/semantically interpretable, and additional robustness checks (different backbone, class imbalance, alternative labeling strategy for Rare Species).
weaknesses: The core theoretical distance DL is explicitly not a formal metric (asymmetric, violates triangle inequality) and relies on a Taylor approximation around a numerically-solved point y1*≈3.016 with an empirically reported mean relative error of 5.3% (max 32.4%) -- this weakens the rigor of the 'existence and uniqueness' claims, since the proven properties apply to the approximated distance, not the exact KL divergence.

The wrapped normal / wrapped-distribution assumptions and the approximation of u1, u3 as simple midpoints mapped via the exponential map at the origin are strong simplifications whose impact on real feature distributions (which are unlikely to be exactly wrapped-normal) is not empirically validated beyond the Taylor-error histogram.

The evaluation is restricted entirely to taxonomic open-set (TOS) classification with existing hierarchical-label datasets (and one BioCLIP-oriented dataset); there is no evaluation on more standard/broader VLM benchmarks (e.g., zero-shot ImageNet variants, retrieval, VQA) to demonstrate that the proposed alignment generalizes beyond taxonomy-structured tasks.

Baselines are somewhat narrow -- principal comparisons are against ProTeCt/MaPLe/PromptSRC and two hyperbolic VLM methods (MERU, HyCoCLIP); other recent hierarchical or entailment-based modality alignment approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., Sastry et al. 2025, BioCLIP2) are not directly compared on the TOS benchmarks.

The method introduces considerable complexity (dual learnable curvatures, golden-section search with implicit differentiation, multiple entailment losses, cross-attention hierarchical feature extraction) which raises reproducibility and practical-adoption concerns; although hyperparameter sensitivity is shown to be modest, the interacting design choices (α, layer choice, curvature init, r) are numerous and the paper does not discuss how practitioners would set these for a new, unseen hierarchical dataset.

Performance gains, while often large on hierarchical-consistency metrics (HCA), are more modest on LA/MTA in several settings, and some improvements over the already-hierarchy-aware ProTeCt baseline are incremental (e.g., low-shot HCA deltas are closer to a few points in several rows of Tables 1-3), suggesting the largest gains are concentrated in specific regimes (larger shot count, Rare Species).
